utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Registrar. Today is Wednesday, the 20th of January, 2010. I'd like to greet the accused, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, and I see that Mr. Pusic is sick, and I also forgot to greet Mr. Stojic. I'd like to greet counsel. I would like to greet the witness as well. I'd like to greet all the members of the OTP, as well as all those assisting us, and I would also like to greet the new Usher, who is with us. So we're going to continue with Mrs. Alaburic's questions, but before that, following the questions which were asked to you, Witness, yesterday, at some point I touched upon the question of the 3.000 Croats who left Bugojno and who went towards the Serbian lines. Tonight I looked at a map -- last night, sorry, I looked at a map --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 4D1483. There's no need to look at it. But before I ask you the question, I'd like to ask you the following: Were you very familiar with the Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Prozor, Kupres region? Are you familiar with this region, because if you don't there's no need for me to ask any further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am not familiar with the region in great detail, but I do know where those towns are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So you're telling me you know where the towns, and I think that's enough for me, and I can ask you -- I mean, enough for me to ask you the question. So there's Bugojno, and then there's a road from which it is possible to go from Bugojno to Prozor going through Gornji Vakuf. So let's say I put myself in the situation of the Croatian offensive, Serb -- the BH Army's offensive --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the Croatians fleeing. Looking at the map, I wonder why they didn't go towards Prozor or Rama? What prevented them from doing so, and why did they go towards the Serbian lines, towards Kupres? Can you please tell me why did they not go towards Prozor, Rama, going through Gornji Vakuf? Do you know why, or maybe you don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. Thank you very much. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my colleagues from the Prosecution. Good morning to all in the courtroom, and to you, Mr. Jasak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us, Mr. Jasak, as an analyst in VOS, what was the zone that you primarily dealt with?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: South-East Herzegovina, with focus on Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sorry, I also work at night, and, you know, some questions come to my mind overnight, and last night I was wondering, when you left Bosnia-Herzegovina to join the Croatian Army in August 1993, unless I'm mistaken, in light of the fact that you were a VOS specialist, and Mrs. Alaburic's question is making me think of this question, as a specialist in military intelligence, why did not you go right away to the Croatian staff to deal with military intelligence? Let me try and explain why I'm asking you that question. I'm fully transparent in my questions. There are never any traps; I say it all; and I'm asking you questions. Now, why am I asking you this question? The reason is the following: When the events relating to the locality of Stupni Do took place, Mr. Tudjman himself at a meeting talked about these events, and I'm quoting from memory here, asking the question to the commander who was there and who could face responsibility for the crimes about Visa Razic [phoen]. So he asks the question to those attending around him, Who is it. So, in fact, he wants to know who is Razic. And then I wondered, when I saw this, well, Mr. Tudjman did not receive reliable intelligence about the commander. How come? Was there a weak point in the intelligence services when in fact there are other documents which show us that he was aware about a number of events? So as I re-read the presidential transcript when Mr. Tudjman shows that he did not have the intelligence and he's asking for the intelligence, with someone like you who worked in the VOS and who did not join the Croat intelligence services, why were not you recruited directly by the Croatian intelligence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I completed the command staff school in Zagreb after working at the HVO. And on the 5th of August, 1994, I was deployed on the southern front. That is the proposal that was made when I was taken into active service, because on the 5th of August, 1994, I was admitted into the active service. They decided after the training I completed in Zagreb that it would be the most necessary thing for me to do to go to join General Marinovic in the operations there. That was the assessment of my superiors, and I don't know why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you just allow me to correct the transcript. In line 11, what is recorded is that the witness said that it was decided that he join General Marinovic in the operations there. The witness actually said the southern front with General Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, as for the southern front, we use it very often in this courtroom. I mean, the notion itself. In which state was this southern front where you were working?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the Republic of Croatia. At the time, that was a part of the operations zone of Split, or, rather, the military district of Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, where was the headquarters of this southern front, in what town?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the southern front was in Dubrovnik, and the staff was at Hotel Splendid.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us go back to 1993. So you primarily analysed the area of the operative zone of South-East Herzegovina. Tell us, did you do this in March, April, and May?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you have any knowledge that in the area of the municipalities of Konjic and Jablanica there was fighting between the HVO and the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, your first knowledge about the conflicts in that area, what could you tell us? When did the first serious conflicts break out in the area?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at your binder now, the chapter that has to do with the Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to note for the Honourable Trial Chamber, if you recall where we stopped yesterday in the first binder, we're going to skip the next chapter about joint commands because I think that we have dealt with it already through Their Honours' questions. There should be blue markers, and you should be able to find 4D438 [Realtime transcript read in error "4D348"]. [In English] Binder 1, yes. [Interpretation] This is the last section in the first binder of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is a document that we've seen several times already in this courtroom, that is to say, information of -- provided by Commander Alic from Konjic on the 23rd of March, 1993. The Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina is reporting to its commander in the 4th Corps that 100 members of the HVO had been captured, that the town was blocked, that life in town is paralysed, and "That we continue with arrests." Mr. Jasak, at VOS did you have any knowledge to that effect, that things were actually happening as they are described in this document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, Mr. Jasak, if we wished to know what was going on in the neighbouring municipality of Jablanica, would it be necessary for us to know what was going on in Konjic or can we quite independently view developments in these two neighbouring municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These two municipalities are interlinked, and they should be looked at jointly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, developments in the areas of Konjic and Jablanica, to the best of your knowledge, can they have any effect on the situation and developments in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Developments in the area of Jablanica and Konjic can affect Mostar, because these two areas are within the operative zone of South-East Herzegovina and within the zone of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do these areas make up a geographic whole, irrespective of the military organisation of any army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Good morning Your Honours, and everybody in and around the courtroom. I don't object to the line of questioning, but I just object to the form of the questions. These questions are being put in a very leading fashion, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague Mr. Kruger. I really am doing my best to be very disciplined and to put questions properly. I hope I haven't overstepped in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, does this area make up some kind of a geographic hole?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This area does make up a geographic hole, and that is why this area was included in a single operative zone, that is to say, it is within a single corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we said that this conflict in Konjic ended in a particular way on the 23rd of March, 1993, but could you please remind us, how did it end?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended by the signing of an agreement on the cessation of this conflict, General Petkovic and the commander of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the conflict truly brought to an end once the agreement was signed?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you're not an officer of the level -- or, rather, now you're a colonel, but at the time you were not an officer at the level of a general, and maybe that's a question I will ask General Petkovic if I have the time, I'm not sure. There are many questions which I'm currently preparing. But I'd like to ask you the question, as you told us that you attended the school in Zagreb, military school, so maybe you have the required skills to answer the question. Now, this document shows that in March the BH Army is undertaking a major action in Konjic as it captures 150 members of the HVO. They blocked the town; the town is paralysed. And the colonel writing the report to Pasalic explains that he is continuing the arrests. So from a military standpoint, this is action taking place. Now, you're in military intelligence. This must have been brought to your knowledge. But in military terms, when such a large offensive occurs, at that time did the HVO sing [as interpreted], that in that geographic area and hence the question raised by Mrs. Alaburic is interesting. It sees that there is continuity to loosen the military grip on Lusic [phoen]. Isn't the HVO itself going to be in a position to conduct an operation, an offensive, that is, in order to loosen the grip on Konjic? In the analysis which you have conducted at the time, I mean, was that conduct or was there a cease-fire right away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this particular date, after the agreement there was a cease-fire during the days that followed, but there were some minor skirmishes. The HVO had far fewer men than the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that area, and the HVO had no capacity to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you're introducing two things which I'm hearing for the first time. You said that the HVO had fewer men, and so if I understand it, they were in a situation of inferiority compared with the 4th Corps, and you added they did not have the capacity to defend themselves. So I'm trying to analyse what you said. It means that in military terms, after the offensive of the BH Army, the HVO was not in a position to attack the 4th BH Corps in Mostar because they did not have the strength, I mean, the assets, the military assets. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I meant when I said -- or, rather, I meant Konjic and Jablanica. As for Mostar, at the time, the HVO was engaged to a large part on the front line against the Army of Republika Srpska. All conflicts were resolved by peaceful means and every effort was may to resolve everything by peaceful means because no one thought it was possible that there would be a total war, because the general belief was that neither the HVO nor the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina can defeat the enemy, the Army of Republika Srpska, independently, on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, a correction to the transcript. I think it will be important for your possible future questions. In line 9, his answer is misrecorded when he said that the HVO was not strong enough to resist the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, can you repeat what towns you meant?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Konjic and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a misrecording of the names. The witness said Konjic and Jablanica. He did not say Konjic and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us, did you say Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Konjic and Jablanica. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So you're telling me that in Jablanica the HVO was not in a position to do anything, to conduct an offensive. Now, what about the cease-fire which took place? According to you, did it take place on request by the HVO or on request of the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The cease-fire took place through the agreement reached by General Petkovic and the representative of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. However, you did not answer because you did not know whose request it was. That's what I understood. And the 150 soldiers who were held, I mean, were they released or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what was discussed was the release of prisoners and negotiations were underway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to say that the transcript misrecorded the number of the document that we've just been discussing. I would like to thank Ms. Tomanovic for noting that the number is 4D438. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So we've been talking about March, and we said that there was fighting and that it was stopped. Do you have any knowledge about any skirmishes or clashes in that area in the beginning of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please share it with us.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the area of Neretvica, in the valley of Neretvica, the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please let's look at the next document, P1803. This is an SIS report dated the 4th of April, 1993. In the third paragraph it says: "In the north-east part of the municipality, in the area of the town of Konjic, there are frequent provocations and even attacks populated by -- against settlements populated by the Croat population." Mr. Jasak, did you know about that, that in the surrounding areas where the population was Croatian that there was skirmishes and clashes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have knowledge to that effect because the area here Ivanci, Pajici, and Vratna Gora is close to the valley of Neretvica. It is to the north-west of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you about the HVO in Konjic and Jablanica, and you said that the HVO had far fewer men than the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To the best of your knowledge, in the area of Konjic and Jablanica, would the HVO be capable of carrying out any attack activities and taking control of these towns and pushing the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina out of the area of Jablanica and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO would not be capable of carrying out any such thing because the HVO did not have the sufficient resources for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The last part of your sentence, Mr. Jasak, is not recorded in the transcript. Could you please tell us, it did not have the strength ...

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not have the strength even if it had wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I have to say again that of course there are certain problems with the transcript, but it is due to the fact that you are -- I mean, both of you are talking very quickly and you do not have the pauses in between the questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having cautioned us, Your Honour. We are going to be even slower.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the next document, 2D775, please. This is a report of the HVO from Konjic, dated the 8th of April, and in that report of the 8th of April it is stated that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is attacking the Goran Stanic barracks in Seonica and that the -- if -- and that the barracks are visibly damaged and that the capacity of the HVO would seriously be affected by that. If you had any specific knowledge with regard to that particular date, could you please share it with us if you knew something was happening in the area of Konjic on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had information indicating that there were activities going on there, but as far as I remember, at the time, a representative of the Main Staff was there, and I think he signed this in that capacity, Mr. Slavko Puljic. He was reporting, covering these clashes, and he tried to talk to representatives of the BH Army in order to somehow allay tensions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned representatives of the BH Army, the BH Army and the HVO. Are we talking about a commission that was established pursuant to an agreement between representatives of the HVO and the BH Army that was supposed to work towards a peaceful solution to the situation and the resolution of all problems?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the commission that was there in the area, representative of the Main Staff and the former official of the Eastern Herzegovina operations and Slavko Puljic, he was there and he signed this. And then he forwarded this from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade Command, but he was also the chief of all branches at the HVO Main Staff. One really wanted to know what the situation was both over there and lower down. Ask Arif what his next snide move might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Next one, 2D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm looking at this document. Here, according to this document, there's been a BH Army attack. Arif Pasalic is being -- is obviously involved. And on the next day, a meeting with EU observers is supposed to take place. This is not the first document you see that shows that when there are "incidents," there are immediately meetings either with observers, with the UNPROFOR that takes -- that take place, because there's always a presence of the international community. Now, given this, in order to know who tells the truth, who is perfidious, and who is playing games, I would like to know whether you were involved in these international meetings at one point in time. Did you ever attend one? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I did not attend these meetings. Nevertheless, what this shows is the hypocrisy of Arif Pasalic, commander of the 4th Corps. In this particular case, Slavko Puljic was specifically assigned as a highly trained officer who had been formally trained in the JNA, and I see that he's still with the federation, BH Federation Army. I think he's possibly the highest ranking ethnic Croat in their ranks. That is the reason I tend to lend credence to what he wrote here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're saying that Arif Pasalic had a hidden agenda, was playing games. Well, obviously here it says the same thing in this document. So everybody is blaming themselves for playing games and having hidden agendas. The Judges will have to see who actually did what. And what is a bit surprising here to me is that in these international meetings there are often high-ranking military who attend. They're extremely competent. And normally they should immediately find out who has a hidden agenda. Let me give you an example: General Morillon who signed a number of documents with Halilovic and Petkovic, do you think that you could play games with a person of -- of this competence? Because this is the problem: Everybody's blaming each other, but the international community is fully involved in all these meetings. And when people, you know, are playing games in front of me or have a hidden agenda, I find out very quickly as far as I'm concerned. So I'd like to know how you can explain the fact that Mr. Pasalic, who might have attended this meeting but who is actually challenged here, it seems that the international community hasn't notice anything regarding his behaviour. How could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know why the international community did not invite him. I do believe, however, that these representatives of the international community hail from better organised systems, and they simply couldn't even begin to imagine that something like that might be happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, was it possible, for example, for Arif Pasalic to sincerely want the situation to calm down, nevertheless, one of his subordinate commanders had other ideas and simply refused to comply with one of Pasalic's orders, continuing to cause incidents and continuing to fight? Would an analysis like that be possible based on your knowledge of the situation within the ranks of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such situations would have been possible, but they could only have continued for a very short time before the commander found out and responded. Nevertheless, if we look at the case in hand, the person who wrote this document knows Mr. Pasalic really well. And who signed this document? Mr. Slavko. I think the person who signed this document really knows what they're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 2D246, please. That is our next document. An order by the commander of the 44th Mountain Brigade from Jablanica, Enes Kovacevic. There is a detailed list of assignments for each of the battalions in this brigade. Let us just mention that the 1st Battalion is to be carrying out offensive operations in the direction of Kosna Luka and Doljani village. The 2nd Battalion, among other things, is to take up positions at Boksevica. The 3rd Battalion inter alia is to take up positions at Aleksin Han, which is in the general direction of Mostar. Now, 4th Battalion is the one that I'm really interested in right now. It reads as follows in relation to the 4th Battalion: "Having completed the mobilisation, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th platoons are to take up positions facing Risovac. The 5th platoon is to remain at Doljani village at the ready in order to perform decisive defence until help arrives. The position at Pajici is to be reinforced by anti-armour weapons and a single platoon in order to control any passing traffic. Once combat operations are underway, stop all passing traffic on the road to Sovici and Doljani." Just try and analyse this, Mr. Jasak. If the BH Army wants to seize some positions facing Risovac, what could possibly be the final objective of this operation?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the BH Army are trying to take up positions facing Risovac, that would imply that the objective is to cut off any help that the Croats might be receiving from the Posusje area, prevent it from getting there, prevent any support from reaching those people at Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Based on this order and your knowledge of the situation as it prevailed, what about these villages mentioned here, Sovici and Doljani? Did they have any military significance for the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sovici and Doljani certainly had a military significance for the BH Army. That was the only access that was still open in terms of reaching Jablanica and helping out the Croats in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The order seems to suggest that the 5th Platoon of the 4th Battalion of the 44th Mountain Brigade of the BH Army was actually in the village of Doljani. Did you know anything about the BH Army and its presence in the village of Doljani?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew something about it. We didn't know it was the 5th Platoon, but we knew they had a military presence there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's try to analyse this. P1874. We shall be using further documents to get a closer read of the situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this document is dated April 14th, 1993. According to the Prosecution, an ultimatum was given for April 15th to ensure that Muslim troops in Croat sectors would come under Croat control and Croat troops under Muslim territories would go -- would be under the control of -- of the BH Army. And normally this was supposed to happen on the 15th of April, 1993. And in his case, the Prosecutor says that it's the HVO who attacked first, which is why we have Doljani and Sovici. That's the Prosecution's case. Mrs. Alaburic is showing you a document which is an order sent to the BH Army and providing for a number of operations to be carried out and mentioning the presence of the BH Army in Doljani. This is what is stated in the document. But I also note the explanations we have in this document. The BH Army seems to have obtained intelligence from different sources, and it seems that for a couple days, i.e., on April 12, 13, and 14, was preparing movements and preparing its units in view of having -- making an operation against the BH Army. So the BH Army seems to be preparing for this operation, which is why we have this order with 14 items. I note item 10, for example, which deals with the war hospital in Jablanica. And in item 10 this order says that the medical care and instruments have to be prepared there. So there are two ways to look at this: Either the HVO attacked first and they are preparing for this attack, or it's the opposite. Now, you're in military intelligence and you're under oath today, so I would like to know what is your opinion. Do you believe that the HVO attacked or the BH Army attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was the BH Army to attack first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, you used the word "believe." You said, 'I believe." Let me ask you now about your specific knowledge in your capacity as a VOS analyst.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question I received from the Chamber was do I believe, and then I said I believe this and I believe that. Our actual knowledge was that the HVO was attacked. Intelligence, such as they used, to the effect that the HVO was attacking them, well, that was exactly the sort of information that they were using in some of their other reports. The whole world knew what happened on the 13th [as interpreted] of June, 1993, in Mostar. It's a similar term being used. Someone else is attacking; they are striking back, taking large portions of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may just correct the date, line 17. The witness did not say the 13th --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One speaker at a time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did not say the 13th of June. The witness said the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I may interpret, I don't think that comes across with particular clarity in the English. Are you trying to say that the BH Army in their reports normally said that the HVO was attacking them and then they responded, and that again was their interpretation of what occurred on the 30th of June, 1993, where beyond a shadow of a doubt the clashes that started were triggered by the BH Army? Is that what you were trying to say?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next document, P1874. This is a joint report of the HVO Main Staff in relation to the 13th of April, 1993. Could you tell us a thing or two by way of introduction, Mr. Jasak? Do you know how these joint reports are produced?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A document like this is normally based on reports arriving from the operation zones, those subordinate to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And the Main Staff does what exactly with these incoming reports from the operation zones?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in most cases they would simply be copied, aside from, perhaps, certain linguistic shortcomings. And it was a useful thing to have them all in one place. That's what this procedure was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you say "copied" or "copied"?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say "copied." I said typed up again, copied by being typewritten.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now we have a good interpretation, "typed up again." I don't know. My impression is Judge Trechsel wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your question, Ms. Alaburic, reads "Did you say copied or copied," and that is probably not what you said. It's two times the same. Is it white or white?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was misinterpreted. I don't wish to further complicate matters and analyse the misinterpretation, so instead of that I simply re-asked the witness the same question. The witness said that the reports from the operation zones were being copied, thereby creating these documents known as joint collective reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again the interpretation is "copied." These were not copied.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The English word for "prepisivati" is to copy, which refers both to handwriting and typewriting. Could someone please share that with counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could someone as an Englishman please give us a hand. Could we say retype the document or retype? I think retype would be retype, yes. Let us then try to use the word retype. We were trying to prove that the documents from the operation zone were retyped, and that's how these joint reports came into existence. Grammatical corrections were sometimes entered, as the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, if you look at this report and look at paragraph 3, saying: "I requested an interim report from the Rama Brigade ordering them to set up all the elements for artillery activity ..." Who is this person speaking here in the first person singular?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the commander of the North-West Herzegovina operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we look at this document, this collective report for South-East Herzegovina, on the 13th of April we received three reports from Konjic. How did this work as a rule? How many reports on a daily basis would be dispatched from the operation zones to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, one report a day. Whenever the need arose, more were dispatched, when there was more happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We see that we have three reports from Konjic for that day. How would you characterise the situation in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the situation was changing every hour. That is why we had three reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have no time to take this one hour at a time. Let us focus on the main conclusion. Report number 3 says this is an all-out attack on the entire Konjic and Jablanica area. Does this allegation tally with the information that you were privy to in the VOS or would you change anything?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't change anything. These reports came from the operation zones. They normally reached both of the OS and the Main Staff, and the substance of these reports was normally the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document, P1879.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I see a document, I try to examine it from the two angles, from the Prosecutor's case and the Defence case. I try to see if there is exculpatory elements and inculpatory elements. It's quite a -- quite an exercise. Now, in this document it seems that there could be some exculpatory elements because there is an all-out attack in the Konjic and Jablanica area. This is written by the commander of the operational zone, because we know that this collective report is a compilation of different reports coming from different operational areas. But I note that there is no number here, no reference number. It's blank. No reference number for the logbook. So starting from this, because this is how a criminal Judge works, you know, you have to scrutinise the details and then add them up. But starting from this detail, the following question could be asked: On April 14, 1993, maybe General Petkovic was busy doing something else, didn't have any time to reports. Maybe he was preparing his own all-out attack for the HVO. And he had other things on his plate than just reading about the situation, which might explain why, on that day, he did not sign or endorse the report, and then the report is not recorded. Just because he's busy doing something else. This is an assumption, of course; I have no element to back it up. But I'd like to know whether you think it is normal for a collective report not to have a reference number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may please try to explain how these reports were produced. All of the reports arriving from the operation zones had their numbers, and they were simply filed away as such. These collective or joint reports are nearly identical. As far as I know, they were meant to be helpful to General Petkovic, to keep him from having to handle too many different documents at the same time. Normally it was General Petkovic's secretary who would put all these reports together. Then if General Petkovic forwarded these reports to anyone else, then she would be one of these signatories. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your explanation is the following: General Petkovic is asking his secretary to make a summary of all of the reports. The secretary does the work and prepares for this document which we see here before us. General Petkovic reads this document and draws the conclusion that he does not have to send this document to other people, and that could explain why there is no reference number. That could be an explanation, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That's right. That's exactly what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, lest there be any misunderstanding, this collective report, is it a summary of the reports from the operative zones or is a -- is this a retyped document from the report of the operative zones?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a literal retyping, but it is a summary so as not to have too much paper, but the content is just like that of the reports. Some came in by telefax. I mean, there are many different ways. So an effort was made to avoid lots of paper. A single report was awaited from general -- a single report was awaited so that when General Petkovic would come back, say, for a trip, he could see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other words. If I understand you properly, it was not a summary of a report, but it simply meant that everything was put together in one single document.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Everything was brought together in one single place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, these reports, finally do they bear the name of General Petkovic regardless of where General Petkovic was at that point in time? Say, he could have been at a conference in Geneva for a couple of days. Do the reports for those days also bear his name?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now look at the next document, P1879. Let us look at the end of the document, the last report from Konjic. Let us try to analyse parts of this document together. What is stated here is that during the night major movements of the Muslim forces were noted towards the strategically very important hill of Boksevica, and then it says who holds that hill practically controls almost all of the valley of the Neretvica. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, this hill of Boksevica, was it really of such importance for this area?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This hill was dominant, and from that hill, one could absolutely control the valley of Neretvica and this road that went from Konjic to Jablanica and Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The report further on says that everything boils down to the following: That the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina wants to take Boksevica. According to your knowledge, would that be the right conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, that would be the right conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, part of the area around Boksevica, is it in the zone of South-West Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- a part of the area around Boksevica is in the area of South-West Herzegovina. That is to say, to the north-west or the west of Boksevica is the zone of North-West Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us see what kind of help they're asking for from Konjic. They say: "That is why we ask you for the following: That the artillery from Risovac plateau operates from Jablanica to Ostrozac and, if possible, against the villages of Mrakovo and Rodici. And in this way, the sabotage Muslim group would be threatened." Tell us, Mr. Jasak, if HVO forces are on the Risovac plateau, from which operative zone would these forces be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These forces would be from the operative zone of South-East Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, for these forces to fire artillery from Jablanica to Ostrozac, could they truly help HVO units in the territory of the Konjic municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could help because in this way they disburden the Neretvica valley and Boksevica, particularly because these two villages, Mrakovo and Rodici, are on the southern part of Boksevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the previously quoted part of this report when we spoke about sabotage groups that are moving towards Boksevica, it says that they leave the villages Mrakovo and Rodici. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, to the best of your knowledge when such localities are defined in such a way, I mean that operations should be carry out against them, why is this being done as a rule? Why are certain localities identified as an objective of combat activity?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because enemy units are in such places that aim to carry out sabotages and threaten Croatian positions. In this particular case, it is Boksevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd like to correct the transcript in line 6. The witness did not say Croatian positions but HVO positions. Let us now look at the next section. It says: "We are asking Prozor to support us with artillery in firing at the objectives that we have already set, including the villages of Sovici and Celina which would cause panic, and if that is not done it would be hard for us to get out of these places." Tell us, to which operative zone is this request for assistance being sent?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This request is being sense to the North-West Herzegovina operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the assumption that it is an undeniable fact that in mid-April 1993 the artillery of the operative zone of North-West Herzegovina operated in the areas of Jablanica and Konjic, what would you tell us on the basis of these documents? What is the objective of the combat activity of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective of the combat activity of the HVO in this area was to disburden the units of the Croatian Defence Council from attacks by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., prevent the total defeat of the HVO in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasak, to the best of your knowledge did the HVO ever plan to attack Jablanica and take control of the Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the HVO had never planned that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, is there any other operative zone near the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Near the municipality of Konjic, there were three zones: the operations zone of South-East Herzegovina; the zone of North-West Herzegovina; and the third one, the operations zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D874. Could we have a look at that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the head of Main Staff, 15th of April, 1993, sent to the operations zone of Central Bosnia. It says in relation to the newly created situation in the municipality of Konjic and the difficult position that the Herceg Stjepan Brigade finds itself in, the order is to have forces from the Central Bosnia operations zone engage forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and then certain positions are specified. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, from a military point of view, is it logical to engage certain units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and -- from the north and in this way make the position easier for the operation zone?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was the only proper thing to do from a military point of view, because if we're talking about the Neretvica valley and this part that other forces came from, Gradina, et cetera, this is the only way in which it could be disburdened. However, as far as I know these units were also facing major problems and there were operations in that area and they could not give any significant assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what is going on in Konjic. 4D83. This is a combat report from a unit of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the end of the document it says: "This time there shall be no stopping. We are going to press ahead until final victory." I am not going to finish ring this sentence because I'd like to analyse only these two elements. Mr. Jasak, as a military analyst, how would you interpret this assertion made by a military commander, "This time there is no stopping"?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we see that intensive combat activity is still underway and we know that on the 23rd of March combat operations had been stopped, those that had been started before that, I would conclude that now they do not wish to stop combat operations until there is a final military defeat of the Croatian Defence Council in the territory of Konjic and Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Jasak, whose nickname was Tetak in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. Sulejman Budakovic had the nickname of Tetak. He was Arif Pasalic's deputy. I knew him personally from the time of the Independent Battalion in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this document it says that a proposal is being made to Tetak to order a cut-off of energy in Croatia and a part of Herzegovina, but we are more interested in the rest, to attack and free Boksevica and Pisvir. To the best of your knowledge, were these localities an objective of the activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these localities were an objective of the attacks of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document now from the point of view of the HVO. 4D453. At the time when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is reporting and saying, "We should not stop until there is final victory," reports are coming in from Konjic that Konjic is under attack. And the last document reads, "Let us move ahead while we are still alive." As a military analyst, can you give us your comment on this sentence? What does it actually mean?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This sentence means that over here the Croatian units are fighting for dear life, and we see that it's been sent to all addresses, not only to the command of the operations zone of South-East Herzegovina that was their immediate superior, but also to the Main Staff and the command of the operations zone of North-West Herzegovina, the HVO, Fojnica, and the brigade of Rama. So you see that this is a reaction of panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the next document, P1882. This is yet another report from the Herceg Stjepan Brigade, the 3rd Battalion from Jablanica. What is stated here is that: "Yesterday, on the 14th of April, around 1500 hours, representatives of the BH Army's Neretva Brigade came in in order to preserve peace in the inhabited areas of Doljani and Sovici, but in our opinion they are just trying to relieve Bosnian army forces that were consequently operate towards Boksevica and towards our forces in the Neretvica valley." Can you give us your comment with regard to this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion was correct. The objective was to disburden the forces of the BH Army. That is to say, to buy time, to ensure peace in the area until everything else was resolved in the Neretvica valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the assessment here is that forces of the BH Army would be freed up by doing this in order to proceed towards Boksevica, does that mean that these forces are in the villages of Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it most certainly means that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who is the other signatory to this document?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomic, who was an official of the intelligence service. He was the assistant battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever read his reports?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because his reports normally came through the South-Eastern Herzegovina operation zone, which then they -- which they then consolidated for the purposes of the Main Staff VOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 3D557 is our next document. The day after, the 16th of April, Arif Pasalic. The introduction states: "In the Neretvica sector, the HVO is facing a difficult situation because they don't have enough men. They want their own artillery from Risovac to pound our positions to the north of Neretvica." Mr. Jasak, assuming that what Mr. Arif Pasalic is saying here is correct, would any request in fact made for the Risovac-based artillery units to pound Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests for the Risovac-based artillery units to pound the villages just beyond Boksevica, specifically the villages from which acts of sabotage were being carried out. I think this actually belongs to Jablanica, or, rather, it's just there on the border.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Jablanica municipality, not the town itself.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the HVO artillery from Risovac were to pound the area just north of Neretvica, what would that lead you to conclude? What would they have been trying to achieve by doing that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was to rescue our units in the Neretvica valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 1 of the order, Article 1, Arif Pasalic says that one should continue fighting in the zones of responsibility of individual units. One should prevent any fresh HVO forces from arriving from the general direction of Prozor through the villages of Kacuni and Grevici and the direction of Bradina as well. Furthermore one should harmonise and consolidate any joint action in order to be as successful as possible in crushing the resistance of the HVO. Based on this document, was is the character of the combat operations being carried out by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are offensive combat operations. They are attacking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll skip a document now and move on to 4D599. 4D455. It's a combat report produced by Esad Ramic. This is a forward command post of the 4th Corps. The situation is described here at certain localities throughout Konjic municipality. What I want to know about is what it says about the last HVO facility in Radesina village. It reads --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's towards the end of the document, the second to last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It reads: "We shall be trying to wrap up the job at Konjic as soon as possible and then use all of our brigades to launch a counter-strike along two axes, the first being Konjic-Jablanica-Mostar; and the other, Konjic-Prozor-Rama." Mr. Jasak, what does it exactly mean to wrap up the job at Konjic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to inflict a total military defeat on the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about launching a counter-strike along two designated axes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means proceed as previously planned down the Konjic-Jablanica-Mostar axis, thereby linking up the three municipal territories in order to create appropriate conditions for continuing to operate further down towards the south, Stolac, Capljina, and the sea coast itself in order to eventually reach Croatia's border. As for Konjic-Prozor-Rama, that would be the other axis, quite simply to prevent any breakthrough by the HVO from the other side in an effort to provide assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, I have a question for you. On the last document I see a figure D1 with a number. I'd like to know where this document comes from. Is it a document which was used in the Naletilic's case where 411 documents were admitted for the Naletilic defence and 80 documents for the Martinovic Defence were admitted? Does this document come from that particular file or does it come from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could you please repeat the document number. It says 1D, and I'm not sure which document you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. I need to look again at the last document. Can you please tell me again what the number is for the last document?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4D599.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you see in 4D599, in the English version it says: "Exhibit D1/340." Now, where does this document come from? Is it a document which comes from the Naletilic-Martinovic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. We tried to study the documents from that case very closely, and we have been trying to use any documents that proved to be of relevance. I hope that we have succeeded in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you just confirmed the Naletilic, Martinovic case?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That is the trial from that document, and that document has already been exhibited in our case as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try to wrap up the Konjic story. 2D89. The date is the 18th of April, 1993. Alija Izetbegovic and Mate Boban are trying to reach an agreement on a cease-fire. In Article 3 they order for all clashes to stop and cease with immediate effect. Mr. Jasak, did you know that soon after the clashes in Central Bosnia and South-East Herzegovina an order was adopted to cease all clashes?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P1959 is our next document, 1959. The order is dated the 18th of April, and the HVO units are here ordered to immediately stop all clashes assumed to the Boban-Izetbegovic Agreement. Mr. Jasak, who signed this order?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was signed by Zeljko Akrap on behalf of General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, to wrap up Konjic. Our next documents, we'll be looking at them briefly and then I'll ask you a single question. On the 18th, the decision was taken to stop all conflicts. 4D445 is our next document. This is a combat report of the BH Army, dated the 18th of April, at 2200 hours. The last paragraph states: "Following your dispatch about the negotiations with the Chetniks at Butmir, Mr. Handzo Mustafa was assigned." Mr. Jasak, was there any information indicating that throughout the clashes in the Konjic and Jablanica region representatives of the BH Army were negotiating about something with this army that they here refer to as the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew about that as early as January. I don't think I ever saw this specific document though.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: There are a number of places mentioned here in the general Konica area that were taken or about to be taken by the BH Army. Did the fighting continue on the 18th of April as well?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the fighting continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 4D90. The 22nd of April, 1993. During the day in Konjic there was intense fighting. One had to give up the idea of liberating certain villages, but the decision was taken to liberate the village of Radesina beforehand. Mr. Jasak, this report dated the 22nd of April, four days after the cease-fire agreement was signed, in your opinion as a military analyst, is this document relevant in terms of understanding what was going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is certainly highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And why would that be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they were agreeing and signing one set of conditions and doing something entirely different in reality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the fighting in fact continue up until the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm skipping a document here. 4D91, another BH Army document, dated the 24th of April. In relation to the 25th of April, we are planning a continuation of our activities along the entire front line and taking the villages of Vrci and Budisina Ravan. Mr. Jasak, could this document be relevant for understanding the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it could. It also shows that there is no compliance with the terms agreed as early as the 18th of April. It's not Budisina Travan. It's Budisina Ravan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you for your opinion, if you believe you know enough about what was going on at the time. Any continuation of these BH Army activities which in itself flew in the face of the cease-fire that was agreed, do you think anything like that would have been possible without the consent of the high-ranking commanders in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing like this could have happened unbeknownst to high-ranking commanders in the BH Army. Maybe something like this could have gone on for a single day, but if anyone had failed to carry out an order actually sign by President Izetbegovic, this person would then have been removed, meaning even President Izetbegovic himself would have known about this, as well as their supreme military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it might be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mrs. Alaburic, you have an hour and 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let us move on to a new section. Your Honours, we are moving on to binder number 2. We'll be discussing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones not being used please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, were you in Mostar in the first half of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where were you during the night between the 8th and 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Mostar, the same place as usual, in a flat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did anything out of the ordinary happen that night as opposed to previous nights?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special except the morning of the 9th I was sleeping and then I was roused by loud detonations from shells exploding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got up and got ready to leave. A friend drove me to the Main Staff. That's how we did things. There were no telephone lines that were working, so whenever you heard something, you would just simply go and report to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that you did not have a telephone in your flat?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What time, roughly speaking, did you reach the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At about 6.00 a.m. on the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any officials already who were up and about at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw about ten different people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was on duty the previous night at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, I saw that Bozo Peric was the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the way from your house to the Main Staff -- well, first of all, tell me how long did it take you to get there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: About five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: While you were driving, could you see from inside the car what was going on outside?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't really see anything, but I heard explosions and shooting, sounds of shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you came to the Main Staff, did you ask anyone there what was going on in Mostar and if they knew anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked the duty officer, and he said, The Muslims have attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did he specify the parts of Mostar in which there was fighting?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said there was fighting around the office of the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna near the roundabout, and also that Sjeverni Logor was under attack, specifically the Tihomir Misic Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you spend any time at the Main Staff that morning? Did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed. I phoned my boss and I asked him what I was suppose to be doing. He told me to try and talk to the electronic activity centre in order to tell them to step up their activities, that's all. He said I should also analyse our reports, specifically those mentioning the possibility of BH Army action being taken against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, Mrs. Alaburic asked you some excellent questions which help us follow what you did almost minute by minute, but she forgot to put a question to you. You arrived at 6.00 a.m., and you told us that you were the advisor to the head of military intelligence, and you told us that your office right next door to his. If I understood you correctly, I believe that your activity was to look into BH Army activities. Well, at 6.00 a.m. suddenly people are telling you the BH Army attacks -- had attack. Well, if I -- this is what I thought: If I was in his shoes, if I had his job, I would wonder whether I had may a professional error because I hadn't detected that the BH Army was about to attack. Did this spring to your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't entirely understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is a bit complex, and I will rephrase it, and I'll go into details. We know that you are an analyst, that you work for military intelligence and you analyse military intelligence. We know that you make reports for your boss using elements that you can collect, and then these reports are conveyed to the line of command. So you work for military intelligence. I assume that since you work -- you are in this line of work, your objective is to find out what the enemy is doing or also what friends are doing, because sometimes, you know, there are friends that are not real friends, et cetera. So you are trying to collect information on what the others are about to do or intend to do or might do. On the night from May 8 to May 9 you were sleeping soundly, and suddenly the BH Army attacks. You arrive at 6.00 a.m. You're told that the BH Army has attacked. So, professionally, don't you think that you might have made a mistake, a professional mistake, because you didn't detect the fact that the BH Army was escalating its activity and planning an attack. Did that come to your mind at one point in time on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that did cross my mind as well. Nevertheless, at the time we were already forwarding information to our own superiors about such a possibility that existed, especially after what had occur in this other operation zone a little further up north. Nevertheless, it is quite obvious to me that our reports were not quite being taken seriously. I know that they were talking to local commanders, and they were saying that they did not believe there was any real danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood my question, and you're answering very accurately. For -- let me tell you for the transcript that you said that earlier you had provided some information because you had detected that up north there were operations underway. You passed on this information to your superiors, but they didn't take you seriously. They didn't believe you. That's what you said; right? Did I sum up what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessarily that they didn't believe us. They were simply confident that the situation in Mostar was a bit more peculiar than over there. They reckoned that we had been working together with them for quite a long time in Mostar by this time. They simply refused to believe that anything like that might come to pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, last week we heard the chief of artillery in Eastern Herzegovina operation zone here in this courtroom. He told us that up until the 8th of May he had been drinking coffee every day with his colleagues in the BH Army Eastern Herzegovina Corps and that they were headquartered in Vranica up until the date the clashes started on the 9th of May. So tell us what you know about the communication between certain HVO officers and certain BH Army officers. Was there any way to envisage that the clashes that erupted on the 9th of May would eventually happen?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you looked at the Mostar area alone, there was nothing to lead anyone to believe that clashes would soon be erupting. Nevertheless, we from the VOS tended to take a broader view of the situation. There had been a number of incidents before, but those were soon dealt with at a local level between the 4th Corps and everyone else; all the problems were quickly dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, the record misstates who was involved on behalf of the HVO. You said the 4th Corps and who else whenever there were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please observe a pause between your questions and your answers to allow the interpreters to interpret correctly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer, Mr. Jasak, and also, could you please pause a little before you start answering my question in order to allow the interpreters to do their job properly. So who were they negotiating with?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were talking to their counterparts from the South-East Herzegovina operation zone and the HVO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the first document that we have covering this topic and then we'll be going back to the 9th of May and what happened. 4D557. 4D557. This is an Arif Pasalic report which he sent to the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the BH Army staff, dated the 20th of April, 1993. It says that a meeting was held of representatives of the BH Army and the HVO. The setting up of joint military and political points was agreed. They agreed to try and stop mutual clashes along the confrontational line along the following axes, Semovac-Bulevar-Mose Pijade, also that joint check-points would be set up, manned also by someone from UNPROFOR and so on and so forth. Mr. Jasak, in late April 1993, was there any co-operation that was being brokered between the BH Army and the HVO in Mostar under the auspices of UNPROFOR? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I know that that was agreed upon, because at night-time there was random shooting in town. In order to know who was on which side, an agreement was reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you have any knowledge about these agreements and all of this that was taking place under the auspices of UNPROFOR? Do you have any knowledge of that affecting the military authorities in Mostar in terms of forecasting what the future behaviour of the BH Army would be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, when this was agreed upon, it was believed that this would lead to a reduction of tensions and that all would turn towards the joint enemy and defence from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 9th of May, 1993, when you came to the building of the Main Staff in the morning, did you see any military commander in the building itself or in the yard?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In passing, I saw Tuta. I saw that some soldiers were walking up to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you hear what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not hear what they were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at 3D3101, please. Let us see whether this description of what happen in Mostar on the 9th of May is correct. This is Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic's book. This is an excerpt from his book. The book is called the "Bosniak-Croatian Political Showdown." Chapter 14, paragraph 1, The War in Mostar. I would be interested in the first two sections of this document.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise to the interpreters. I'm sure that it sounds very bad in their headphones when I accidentally hit the microphone while leafing through these pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Mr. Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I knew Mr. Hadziosmanovic personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was he involved in politics in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the representative of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: President or representative?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He says that -- he said the following: "I was an eyewitness of that war in Mostar from the spot where my apartment was located. In settlement centre number 2, I could clearly see heavy machine-guns of HVO firing from the locality of Hum hill towards the locality of Semovac, Bulevar, around --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you're too fast, much too fast. I'm sorry. When you read, there's always a danger that you go downhill. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise primarily to the interpreters and then to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So: "... Semovac, Bulevar, around the health care centre and towards the high school where the 4th Corps units are crossing Bulevar and getting to Liska Ulica, towards the locality of Liska Street. The most intense infantry attacks of the 4th Corps combatants were Musala - the new pontoon bridge - the former street of Korzo, as -- and then there were also some smaller attacks from Cernica Street across Bulevar, it was the health care centre, and the gardens nearby. In those moments of the 4th Corps combatants infantry attack, heavy machine-guns of the HVO fired towards Bulevar and the buildings located by the road itself. Another part of the heavy machine-guns fired towards the localities of Vranica building in Stjepana Radica Street where the command of the 4th Corps was located. Heavy artillery weapon of the HVO severely fired towards the temporary establishments of the BH Army between 8 and 9 o'clock, the building of the hygiene institute, the SDK, and Konak. Artillery fire towards these localities alternated in waves. At the same time, one could hear artillery explosions on localities of Bijeli Brijeg towards Cim and Rudnik. Localities of Bijeli Brijeg towards Cim and Rudnik. That was coming from the left bank and targets were being hit which were marked by previous orders of the 1st Mostar Brigade commander, dated the 20th of April, 1993." Let us look at one of the documents in this respect, the document of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, date the 20th of April. There are a few of them. We're just going to look at one. 2D478. So we are skipping the next document after the quotation from the book, so it is document 2D478, or an order by Mr. Midhat Hujdur, commander of the Mostar Brigade of the HVO, in which targets are being specified, namely Cekrk; Nova Banka; and the high school, Gymnazia; and then the Avenija Rudnik area; and then Bijeli Brijeg; Rondo; and the university; and then the tower at Hum is mentioned.
